abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces the Hierarchical Communicating Vector Machines (HCVM), a novel computational model that fundamentally reimagines concurrent computation by integrating hierarchical state spaces with message-passing semantics. Unlike traditional process algebras such as CSP and CCS, which treat all interactions uniformly, HCVM organizes computation into nested layers where inter-layer communication follows distinct semantic rules from intra-layer interactions. We establish the formal foundations of HCVM through a complete operational semantics based on labeled transition systems, demonstrating that the model possesses greater expressiveness than existing process calculi while maintaining decidability properties for essential behavioral equivalences. A central contribution lies in proving that HCVM can capture both dataflow and control-flow concurrency patterns within a unified framework, resolving a long-standing dichotomy in the theory of parallel computing. We further develop a notion of hierarchical bisimulation that enables compositional reasoning about complex concurrent systems. The theoretical framework presented herein opens new avenues for specification and verification of modern computing systems exhibiting hierarchical organization, including distributed operating systems and modular software architectures. Our results suggest that the hierarchical perspective offers a more natural abstraction for reasoning about computation in complex, multi-layered systems.

We present a refined analysis of the dynamic graph connectivity problem under fully dynamic edge insertions and deletions, achieving substantial improvements over existing algorithmic bounds. While previous approaches to this fundamental problem in distributed computing achieved amortized costs of O(√n) or O(log² n) per operation, we develop a novel decomposition technique based on sparse graph separators that yields O(log n · log log n) worst-case time per operation. Our method combines elements from the earlier Frederickson and Gibson-Schings algorithms with a new hierarchical clustering approach that maintains a certificate structure more efficiently than prior constructions. We provide rigorous proofs of correctness and amortized complexity, demonstrating that our algorithm maintains a spanning forest certificate of size O(n log n) while supporting edge updates in the improved time bounds. Additionally, we prove lower bounds showing that any algorithm achieving sublogarithmic performance must use randomization or make assumptions about the input distribution. The improved bounds have direct implications for network routing, incremental clustering algorithms, and real-time graph processing systems where worst-case guarantees are essential for reliability analysis.

We present Cascade, a novel distributed computing framework that fundamentally shifts the paradigm for implementing large-scale stream processing applications. Traditional stream processing engines rely on dataflow graphs with static topologies, which inadequately capture the dynamic reconfiguration requirements of modern edge computing scenarios. Cascade introduces adaptive topology synthesis, where computation graphs are dynamically constructed and reconfigured based on workload characteristics and resource availability without interrupting processing. The framework is grounded in a new theoretical model of stream computation called Parameterized Dataflow, which extends classical Kahn process networks with run-time parameterization of communication channels and processing elements. We provide a complete specification of the Cascade runtime system, including protocols for topology discovery, dynamic load balancing, and fault-tolerant checkpointing that preserve exactly-once processing semantics. Implementation on commodity hardware demonstrates that Cascade achieves 3-5x throughput improvements over Apache Flink on workloads exhibiting bursty patterns, while maintaining sub-millisecond reconfiguration latency. The architecture enables novel applications in edge analytics, IoT data fusion, and adaptive scientific simulations that were impractical under static dataflow paradigms.

This paper presents an optimized implementation of concurrent skip lists that substantially improves lock-free synchronization performance for multi-core systems. While skip lists provide excellent average-case complexity for ordered operations, existing lock-free implementations suffer from excessive contention and ABA problem overhead that degrade performance under high concurrency. Our design, called TurboSkip, incorporates several novel techniques: a hierarchical back-off strategy that adapts to contention patterns, a specialized memory reclamation scheme based on epoch-based reclamation with epoch fusion, and a new node layout that reduces cache-line contention during traversals. We provide a complete formal specification of the TurboSkip algorithms and prove their correctness through mechanized verification using the Iris framework. Performance evaluation on 64-core systems shows throughput improvements of 2.8x over the best prior lock-free skip list implementations for mixed read-write workloads, with particularly significant gains (up to 6x) for range query operations that are critical in database index structures. The improved performance extends to specialized workloads including priority queue simulations and sorted set operations. We discuss how TurboSkip can serve as a drop-in replacement for balanced tree data structures in concurrent applications, with additional benefits in implementation simplicity.
